question: A patient with an infected finger abscess (tissue pH ~6.0) receives lignocaine infiltration but achieves minimal pain relief. What is the pharmacokinetic explanation?

answers.text: At pH 6.0, the ionised (BH⁺) form predominates — less unionised drug penetrates the axonal membrane, reducing block efficacy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Local anaesthetics exist in pH-dependent equilibrium between ionised (BH⁺, hydrophilic) and unionised (B, lipophilic) forms. The unionised form penetrates the nerve membrane. At pH 6.0, the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation shifts equilibrium heavily toward BH⁺, dramatically reducing the effective intracellular drug concentration.

answers.text: Bacterial toxins in infected tissue directly inactivate lignocaine molecules

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Bacterial toxins do not directly inactivate LA molecules. The failure is physicochemical — the acidic pH of infected tissue traps LA in its ionised, membrane-impermeable form, preventing adequate nerve penetration.

answers.text: Infected tissue has increased Na⁺ channel density requiring more drug to achieve blockade

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Na⁺ channel density does not significantly increase in infected tissue. The problem is inadequate drug delivery to existing channels because the acidic environment traps LA in its ionised form.

answers.text: Inflammation upregulates local esterase activity, rapidly metabolising lignocaine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Lignocaine is an amide LA metabolised by hepatic CYP enzymes, not local esterases. Even ester LAs are hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterases, not tissue-level enzymes upregulated by inflammation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key principle: LA efficacy depends on the unionised form penetrating the nerve membrane. At low tissue pH (infection), more LA exists as ionised BH⁺ → less membrane penetration → reduced block.
Well done. The pH–ionisation relationship is the key to understanding LA failure in acidic tissue — consider nerve block proximal to the infection when infiltration fails.
